title: Warnings, cards and penalties
summary: How penalties work in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting. First a warning with a yellow card; a red card for repeating an offence on the stand; jury sanctions, up to exclusion, for other repeats and serious misconduct.

body.html: FITASC penalties get heavier step by step. By entering a competition, you accept the rules and the penalties. The first time you break a rule, you normally get a warning, shown with a yellow card. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ a classic example is the gun position. A stock above the line on the vest, or a gun mounted before the target appears, earns a spoken warning and a yellow card.

html.sporting: Repeating an on-stand offence on the same layout after the warning (gun position or early mount, the time limit, shooting at a declared No Bird) brings a red card. A single is scored zero; doubles follow the table in the rules guide.
html.compak: Repeating an on-stand offence on the same Compak® Sporting layout (the field where you are shooting) after the warning brings a red card. This covers the time limit, refusing a target, shooting at a declared No Bird and the malfunction rules. A single is scored zero; doubles follow the table in the rules guide.

body.html: The same scale applies to shooting at a declared No Bird and to going over the time limit; see The call, time limits and lateness.

Coaching, that is, someone giving you advice or instructions while you compete, is penalised too. You get a yellow card, repeats are sanctioned by the jury, and the referee sends the person who coached out of the shooting area.

Other repeat offences (for example dress, competitor number, coaching or conduct) go to the jury, the competition's panel of officials. So do refusal to comply (not following the referee's decisions) and an attempt to influence the referee. The jury can score one target as lost, strike out a whole round of 25 targets, or exclude you from the competition. Throwing a gun, abuse or violence, and deliberately shooting at live animals can mean immediate exclusion. An exclusion stays on FITASC's record for five years and brings no refund.
After a final ruling, resume shooting and let it go. Disputing the ruling after shooting has resumed, or criticising it openly, counts as an attempt to influence the referee.
If you disagree with a ruling, protest at once on the stand: raise your hand and say 'protest' or 'appeal'. How protests and jury appeals work is in Results, protests and appeals.
A yellow card is not the end of your round. Many coaches suggest one calm breath, a quick look at what caused it, and then your usual routine. More in Reset after a miss.

notes.html: For an interpreter, the coaching card matters most: in competition, translate only official words, not advice.
Translate 'warning', 'yellow card' and 'red card' literally, calmly and at once.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.en: Warning — your stock was above the line.
phrases.meaning: Sporting™: the gun was too high before the target appeared; next time on this layout it costs the target.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.meaning: An official first warning; it is recorded.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.en: Red card — the target is zero.
phrases.meaning: A repeated offence on the stand: the target is scored as lost.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.meaning: The shooter took longer than allowed (in Sporting™ 15 s between targets, in Compak® Sporting 10 s to call).

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.en: Sir, please leave the shooting area.
phrases.meaning: The referee is removing someone, for example a person caught coaching.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.meaning: Referee warning: coaching is forbidden in competition.

key_points.html: First breach: a warning with a yellow card.
Repeating an on-stand offence on the same layout (for example gun position or the time limit): a red card, and the target is scored as lost. Other repeats go to the jury.
Coaching in competition: a yellow card for the shooter, and the person who coached must leave the shooting area.
Jury sanctions go from the loss of a target or a round up to exclusion, which stays on record for five years.
Disagree? Protest at once on the stand, hand up, before the next call.

did_you_know.html: A second exclusion within three years of the first can lead FITASC to ban a shooter from its competitions for good.

quiz.q: The referee sees a coach giving advice to a shooter during a competition. What do the rules say?

options.text: A red card for the coach
A yellow card for the shooter

quiz.explain: Both rulebooks give the shooter a yellow card, and the person who coached has to leave the shooting area.

quiz.q: Sporting™: after a yellow card for an early mount, the shooter mounts early again on the same layout, on a single. What follows?

options.text: A red card and a zero

quiz.explain: After the first warning, doing it again on the same layout means a red card; on a single the target is zero.

quiz.q: Which of these can the jury NOT impose under the penalty scale?

options.text: A cash fine to the referee

quiz.explain: The jury can take away one target or a whole round, or exclude the shooter; there is no fine to the referee.
